lead: Software measurement replaces opinion with numbers. A team says the project is going well; a metric says it has used 15% more effort than planned and removed 80% of its defects before release. Measurement matters because plans, reviews and estimates improve when someone records what actually happened. Teams size bids, track sprints, judge whether a build is safe to release, and check whether a process change worked.
prereq: You need: 6.1 Management spectrum and project planning for the plan these numbers measure, and the process framework from Unit 1 (see Unit 1, Foundations: Software and Process Models).

blocks.text: A measure is a number produced by a counting rule you write down before you count. Defects found in review is a measure. The rule fixes what counts as a defect, which reviews are included, and the unit. Without a written rule, two people counting the same project produce two numbers and then argue about the numbers instead of the project.

A metric is a measure with a scale and a purpose: a ratio, a rate, or a count per unit of size. Some syllabi state it as the degree to which a system, component or process possesses a given attribute. Defects per KLOC is a metric; 1,200 defects is only a measure. An indicator is a small set of metrics read together to answer one management question, such as whether this build is safe to ship.

items: Name the metric and the question it answers, in one sentence.
Write the counting rule: what is counted, what is excluded, and the unit (defects per KLOC, hours, rupees).
Name the data source and the person who records it.
State the threshold and the action: at what value does the team change something?

blocks.text: Software metrics fall into three domains, and mixing them is the commonest error here. Process metrics belong to the organisation and outlive any single project; they show whether the way of working is improving. Project metrics belong to one project and are read while it runs. Product metrics describe the artefact being built: its size, defects, complexity and behaviour.

Process metrics include defect removal efficiency, review rate in pages per hour, rework as a percentage of total effort, and phase containment, which is the percentage of defects injected in a phase that are also removed in that same phase: defects found in phase i ÷ defects injected in phase i × 100%.

blocks.where: DRE is defect removal efficiency; D_before is defects found before delivery (reviews plus testing); D_after is defects reported by users after delivery. A value near 100% means few defects escaped.

blocks.text: Project metrics include effort variance, schedule variance, cost variance and change requests per phase. They are reviewed weekly and answer whether the plan from 6.1 still holds.

blocks.where: EV is effort variance; E_actual is person-days used; E_planned is person-days planned. A positive value is an overrun, a negative value is an underrun.

blocks.text: Product metrics include defect density, mean time between failures, cyclomatic complexity and response time under load. Defect density normalises defects by size so two products compare.

blocks.where: D is defects counted in a stated window; S is product size in KLOC (thousands of lines of code) or in function points. The unit is defects per KLOC or per function point, and it must be stated.

sections.h3: Goals, leading indicators and quality attributes

blocks.text: The goal-question-metric idea, usually written GQM, keeps measurement honest. You state a goal with a purpose, an issue, an object and a viewpoint; derive three to five questions that would tell you whether the goal is met; then choose one metric per question. A metric that answers no question is dropped, because every count costs effort and invites argument.

Leading indicators move before the outcome, so you can still act: requirement churn, review coverage, open high-severity defects, build success rate. Lagging indicators report after the fact: post-release defects, final cost overrun, customer-reported outages. A dashboard needs both. The leading number tells the team what to change this week; the lagging number confirms whether last month's change worked.
Quality attributes are measured through the questions they answer; reliability uses mean time between failures and availability.
MTBF = MTTF + MTTR;  Availability = MTTF ÷ (MTTF + MTTR) × 100%
blocks.where: MTTF is mean time to failure; MTTR is mean time to repair; MTBF is mean time between failures; availability is the fraction of time the system is usable. Times are in hours.

examples.question: A team planned 200 person-days of effort and used 230. Reviews and testing found 120 defects before delivery; users reported 30 more in the first six months after release. The product size is 25 KLOC. Compute (a) effort variance as a percentage of plan, (b) defect removal efficiency, and (c) defect density per KLOC.
steps: Data: E_planned = 200 person-days, E_actual = 230 person-days, D_before = 120 defects, D_after = 30 defects, S = 25 KLOC.
Effort variance: 230 − 200 = 30 person-days over plan; (30 ÷ 200) × 100% = 15%. Positive means an overrun.
Total defects that ever appeared: 120 + 30 = 150 defects.
DRE = 120 ÷ 150 × 100% = 80%. One defect in five escaped to users.
Split for insight: 120 ÷ 25 = 4.8 per KLOC before release; 30 ÷ 25 = 1.2 after.
examples.answer: Effort variance is 15% over plan, DRE is 80%, and defect density is 6 per KLOC (4.8 before release, 1.2 after).
examples.check:
planned = 200
actual = 230
pre = 120
post = 30
kloc = 25
ev = (actual - planned) / planned * 100
dre = pre / (pre + post) * 100
dens = (pre + post) / kloc
print(round(ev, 1))
print(round(dre, 1))
print(round(dens, 1))

traps: Using a product metric as a process metric. Defect density describes the product; DRE describes how well the process removed defects. Label the domain first.
Computing DRE with review defects only. Leaving out the 30 post-release defects gives 120 ÷ 120 = 100%, hiding every escaped defect.
Sliding the base of effort variance. Divide by E_planned, not E_actual: 30 ÷ 230 gives 13.0%, not 15%. Keep the sign: positive is overrun.

Mixing units in defect density. 150 defects ÷ 25,000 lines = 0.006 defects per line, which is the same as 6 defects per KLOC. The error is writing that answer as "per KLOC"; divisor and unit must match. State the unit every time.
Treating a lagging indicator as leading. Post-release defect counts tell you what already happened; they cannot change this week's build.

quiz.q: Define measure, metric and indicator, with one example of each.
quiz.a: A measure is a raw number from a counting rule (120 defects found). A metric is a measure with a scale or ratio (4.8 defects per KLOC). An indicator is a set of metrics read together for a decision (DRE 80% with density under the team's threshold: ship).

quiz.q: Write the formulas for effort variance and defect removal efficiency, defining every term.
quiz.a: EV = (E_actual − E_planned) ÷ E_planned × 100%, where E_actual and E_planned are person-days used and planned. DRE = D_before ÷ (D_before + D_after) × 100%, with D_before defects found before delivery and D_after defects reported after.

quiz.q: Why does attaching a defect count to an individual's appraisal damage the metric?
quiz.a: People then optimise the number, not the quality: defects get logged as features, small defects go unrecorded, reviews report fewer findings. The measure stops reflecting the work. Attach metrics to the process and the team, with a written counting rule.

quiz.q: A release had 90 defects found in reviews and testing and 10 reported by users. Compute DRE and say what it means.
quiz.a: D_before = 90, D_after = 10, total = 100. DRE = 90 ÷ 100 × 100% = 90%. Nine of every ten defects were removed before delivery; one in ten escaped.

quiz.q: A server has MTTF = 990 hours and MTTR = 10 hours. Compute MTBF and availability.
quiz.a: MTBF = 990 + 10 = 1000 hours. Availability = 990 ÷ 1000 × 100% = 99%, so the system is unusable about 1% of the time.

quiz.q: A team's defect density falls from 5 to 2 per KLOC while post-release defects rise. What could explain this, and what would you check?
quiz.a: Either the product is genuinely cleaner before release or the counting rule changed, for example fewer reviews logged or severity thresholds raised. Check review coverage, review rate, post-release defects by severity, and whether the size measure changed. Falling pre-release density with rising escapes points to weaker reviews, not better code.

quiz.q: Apply goal-question-metric to the goal of reducing rework. State the goal, two questions and one metric each.
quiz.a: Goal: reduce rework effort over the next two releases, from the project manager's viewpoint. Question 1: how much effort goes into rework now? Metric: rework person-days ÷ total person-days × 100%. Question 2: which phase injects the defects that cause rework? Metric: percentage of defects traced to each phase. Threshold: act if rework exceeds 20% of effort or one phase injects more than half the rework.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry dashboards lean on the four DORA measures: deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate and time to restore service. Static analysis tools compute complexity, duplication and code smells on every commit. Researchers study metric gaming, sometimes called Goodhart effects, in defect counts and velocity. Search for GQM, DORA metrics or software analytics.
